planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings, or pot up offsets, in spring in gritty cactus mix in full sun for the deepest near-black tone.

directions: Gothika forms a compact rosette whose foliage shifts from dusky green to deep burgundy or nearly black under strong, direct sun, making it one of the darkest echeverias commonly offered by specialty growers. Keep it dry between thorough soakings in sharply draining mineral mix, since overwatering or shade both wash out the moody coloring and cause stretched, rotted growth. It offsets readily around the base, so established clumps are easy to divide into new starts within a season or two.

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty mix in full sun; a shrubbier, branching habit sets this Oaxacan species apart from rosette-only echeverias.

directions: Unlike most echeverias, Ruby Slippers branches on fuzzy stems rather than staying a single flat rosette, with velvety green leaves edged and tipped in crimson that intensifies under direct sun, drought stress, or cool nights. Orange, bell-shaped flowers rise on short stalks through winter, a bloom season that's unusual for the genus. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil and prune leggy stems back hard in spring to keep the habit full, since the tip cuttings root easily and give you free new plants.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty succulent mix in full sun for the strongest pink-violet color.

directions: Dusty Rose carries wide, spoon-shaped leaves coated in a soft waxy farina that gives the whole rosette a muted pink-to-violet bloom, deepening wherever light is brightest. Offsets form slowly compared with many echeverias, so plan on leaf or stem cuttings if you want to multiply a plant quickly rather than waiting on pups. Give it the driest possible routine in gritty mineral soil, since the thick, water-storing leaves scar and rot fast if the pot stays damp.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty mix in full sun to bring out the cinnamon-toned leaf curl.

directions: Churro's tightly packed, inward-curving leaves take on warm cinnamon, rose, and soft green tones that saturate further with bright, direct sun, and the playful name nods to the leaves' curled, pastry-like shape. It grows taller and narrower than many flat-rosette echeverias, so group several in a shallow pot rather than relying on one plant to fill space. Keep the gritty mix bone dry between waterings and separate basal offsets once rooted to start new clumps.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings or pot up offsets in spring in gritty mix in full sun; parentage of this hybrid is undocumented in trade listings.

directions: Seaglass earns its name from a bright yellow-green rosette lightly marbled with paler green, the wide paddle-shaped leaves dusted in a waxy farina that gives the color an underwater, translucent quality in strong light. Pink, bell-shaped flowers rise on slim stalks in the warmer months above the low rosette. Let the gritty mineral soil dry out fully between waterings, and divide the offsets that form readily around the base to start new pots.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up offsets in spring in gritty mix in full sun; a large-growing hybrid that eventually forms a short trunk as lower leaves drop.

directions: Giant Blue builds one of the larger rosettes in cultivation, its ruffled grey-blue leaves developing bright pink margins under intense sun and, with age, a short exposed stem as older leaves drop below the growing tip. Because the rosette outgrows small pots quickly, give it generous spacing from the start rather than transplanting a cramped plant later. If a rosette stretches or gets leggy, behead and re-root the top in fresh gritty mix; the stump usually resprouts new offsets.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty mix in full sun to bring out the red leaf margins.

directions: Moonshine's thick, minty-green leaves fade to a pale, almost luminous center while the margins flush fiery red, a contrast that sharpens under cool nights and bright, unfiltered sun. Pink flowers appear on arching stalks during the growing season above the tidy, symmetrical rosette. Water deeply until it drains, then let the gritty mineral mix dry out completely, since the waxy leaves hold moisture well and are quick to rot in soggy soil.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty mix in full sun; a patented cultivar (US Plant Patent PP33,617) that rarely offsets on its own.

directions: Angel Kissed forms a dense, full rosette of greyed-green leaves flushed purple with red margins, bred by Renee O'Connell for Altman Specialty Plants. It rarely produces offsets, so leaf or stem cuttings are the dependable way to multiply it. Protected under US Plant Patent PP33,617, it's a newer introduction worth watching for distinctive color saturation that holds even in a small pot. Keep it in bright, direct light and let the gritty mix dry fully between waterings to preserve the compact, non-stretched form.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings or separate offsets in spring in gritty mix in full sun for the strongest red flush.

directions: Victor is a small, tidy Echeveria setorum hybrid whose jade-green rosette flushes cherry red along the leaf faces under strong light, staying compact enough for a windowsill collection. In spring and summer it sends up tall, wiry stalks carrying fire-red and yellow bicolor flowers that stand well above the low foliage. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil and let it dry out completely between waterings, dividing the basal offsets once they've rooted to start new plants.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty mix in full sun for the deepest pastel pink color.

directions: Lilac Spoon's pastel pink leaves end in a distinctive indented, spoon-like tip rather than the usual pointed end, giving the small rosette an unusual, almost sculpted look among collector succulents. Color can shift toward blue-green with cooler weather or less intense light, so strong, direct sun keeps the pink tones and compact shape at their best. Orange flowers appear on short stalks in spring and summer, and offsets forming around the base are easy to remove and root into new starts.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings or pot up offsets in spring in gritty mix in full sun; a widely traded cultivar name without formal botanical registration.

directions: Dama Rosa, Spanish for 'Pink Lady,' forms a tight, rose-like rosette of silvery blue-gray leaves rimmed in blushing pink, the margin color deepening with bright, direct sun. It's a commercially established trade name across specialty succulent nurseries even though it has never been formally registered with a cultivar authority. Water thoroughly and then let the gritty mineral mix dry out completely before watering again, and separate the offsets it forms at the base once they have their own roots.
